title: Making Immersive LLM Chat Experiences More Accessible
text:
Making Immersive LLM Chat Experiences More Accessible

As LLM chat patterns become more widespread, making them accessible is essential to ensuring everyone can access the information, tools, and opportunities they offer. Drawing on his work improving these interfaces, Eric Bailey shares practical ways to make chat-based experiences on the web more accessible and usable for people who rely on assistive technology.

title: Modern CSS Might Make Your Front-End More Complex
text:
Modern CSS Might Make Your Front-End More Complex

Replacing JavaScript with a modern CSS feature can simplify a piece of code while making the wider application harder to reason about. Gabriel Shoyombo explores what happens when logic is split between CSS and JavaScript, sharing practical guidance to help you keep complexity in check during migration.

title: Otherwise you’re just a machine
text:
Otherwise you’re just a machine

AI is getting better at design. Designers should too.

I spend a lot of time looking at design work. Reviewing portfolios. Hiring designers. Working with design leaders, seniors and juniors. Sitting in critiques. Watching people explain how they arrived at a solution. And over time, you start to notice what separates the really good ones.

AI is making that difference both harder to see and more important. A designer can turn an idea into a polished prototype in minutes. They can generate interfaces, write copy, synthesise research, explore directions, vibe code a working experience, and iterate at a speed that would have been unimaginable only a few years ago. That is extraordinary. And to be clear: this is not an argument against any of it. AI literacy is indisputably part of the job.

But something has been bothering me. Recently, reviewing work with my own team, I found myself thinking: I would rather see a great idea drawn on a piece of paper than a beautifully vibe-coded prototype solving the wrong problem.

One shows me how well you can produce. The other shows me how well you can think. And as the quality of what anyone can produce rises, that distinction matters more. The tool should accelerate your thinking. It shouldn’t replace it.

Strangely, one of the best illustrations of this has nothing to do with design. In 2017, María Lorena Ramírez, a Rarámuri runner from Mexico, won a 50-kilometre ultramarathon wearing traditional clothing and huarache sandals. Around her were runners equipped for modern endurance sport. Specialist shoes. Technical clothing. Equipment designed to improve performance. Lorena didn’t prove that those things were useless. She proved something much more interesting. The tools can improve the runner. They cannot make the runner.

Underneath the equipment still has to be endurance. Judgement. Instinct. Discipline. Thousands of hours of capability built long before race day. I think design is similar. Our tools are getting extraordinarily good. We should get extraordinarily good at using them. But there still has to be a designer underneath. That is the designer I am interested in.

Craft: Turning knowledge into mastery

I once worked with a designer who knew an extraordinary amount about design. He read constantly. He knew the latest books, frameworks, UX principles and human-centred design vocabulary. You could have a great conversation with him about almost anything in our field. But when it came to doing the work, something was missing. The depth of his knowledge simply wasn’t reflected in the quality of what he made.

Knowing about design is not the same as being good at design. I think that difference gets to the heart of craft. For me, craft is literacy multiplied by dexterity. Literacy is knowing your discipline: its foundations, principles, rules, references and techniques. Dexterity is being able to put that knowledge into practice: to make decisions, solve problems and consistently produce quality. You need both.

There is a reason mastery takes time. In 1993, psychologist Anders Ericsson and his colleagues studied violin students at a music academy in Berlin. The strongest performers had accumulated thousands of hours of deliberate practice: playing, listening, correcting and playing again. The research would later inspire the famous “10,000-hour rule”, although Ericsson never claimed there was a magic number. What mattered was the practice.

Mastery is built over time, through repetition, correction and refinement. You can learn to read the notes relatively quickly. Making the violin sing is something else entirely.

And that’s what was missing in the designer I worked with. He could read the score. He struggled to play the violin. You don’t develop craft by knowing more about design. You develop it by designing. By making something, looking critically at what you made, correcting it and making it again. By paying attention to the details nobody asked you to care about. By doing it often enough that knowledge starts becoming ability. The tools will change. They always have. And they will make it easier to produce things that look finished. But finished is not the same as good, and production is not the same as mastery. Know your craft. Then practise it until you master it.

Taste: Knowing what good looks like here

Industrial designer Raymond Loewy spent his career trying to understand a contradiction in human behaviour: we are attracted to what is new, but suspicious of what is too new. He called his answer MAYA, Most Advanced Yet Acceptable. Push too little and the work feels familiar. Push too far and people reject it. Somewhere between the two is a moving line. That line, for me, is taste.

I started developing mine very early in my career. My first design jobs were for small businesses around the village where I grew up: a logo, a brochure, whatever needed designing. I remember spending an entire day working on a logo, looking at it at the end of the day, then comparing it with the best work I knew. Mine wasn’t good enough. So I would go home and keep working. Nobody was asking me to compete with the best designers in the world. The client probably wasn’t expecting it either. But I was. I was training my eye before I really knew that was what I was doing.

You develop taste by feeding it. Great design. Bad design. Art, architecture, fashion, film, typography, products, interfaces.

You look, compare, question and criticise. You benchmark yourself against the best. But exposure alone isn’t taste. Knowing what Apple does doesn’t mean copying Apple. Knowing what is trending doesn’t mean following the trend. Taste is knowing what good looks like here.

I still experience that tension regularly when presenting work. Bring something too close to what people already know and the reaction is: What’s new? We’ve seen this before. Push it too far and you get the opposite: No. This isn’t us. The work is finding the cursor between the two. And that cursor moves with the audience, the culture, the product and the moment. That’s why taste isn’t simply preference. It is judgement. Knowing what good looks like, knowing what belongs, and knowing how far to push it.

Instinct: The judgement you can’t yet explain

When I was studying for my master’s in graphic design, I attended a class with Olivier Nineuil, a French typographer who has created typefaces for major brands, including Air France. He told us that during a client briefing, while everyone was talking, he would sometimes make a tiny sketch in the corner of his notebook. Then came the real work: weeks of exploration, drawing, questioning and refining. And quite often, the final direction would end up remarkably close to that first little sketch. I remember finding that fascinating. How could someone see the answer before the process had even begun?

Years later, leading design teams, I sometimes see the opposite behaviour. “But we haven’t done the research yet.” I hear it as though having an idea before interviewing users is somehow bad design practice. I categorically disagree. Of course, research is essential. Talk to users. Observe them. Challenge what you think you know. But don’t go to research empty-handed. Bring an idea. Bring a hypothesis. Bring a conviction worth testing. Evidence should challenge your judgement, not replace the responsibility to have one.

Somewhere along the way, I think parts of modern UX have taught designers to be suspicious of their own judgement.

We have become so concerned with proving every decision that we sometimes forget we are also expected to make decisions. The point is not to be right from the beginning. The point is to have a point of view, and the humility to change it when the evidence tells you otherwise. And not every gut feeling deserves the same trust. Instinct develops through practice, exposure, mistakes, feedback and years of making decisions. Instinct is experience operating faster than explanation. Trust your gut. But listen to users.

Which brings me back to Olivier Nineuil and that little sketch. What looked almost magical to me as a student was not magic. It was a lifetime of looking, drawing, questioning and learning, compressed into a few pencil strokes. The first sketch wasn’t the product of a few minutes. It was the product of all the years that came before it.

Creativity: Making unexpected connections

In 1995, Pixar released Toy Story, the world’s first fully computer-animated feature film. It brought together two worlds that had largely developed separately: computer graphics and the art of storytelling. Pixar’s achievement wasn’t simply a better tool. It was a new way to make films. And I think that’s a useful way to understand creativity. We often talk about creativity as inventing something from nothing. But many of the most original ideas come from connecting things that already exist in ways nobody had thought to connect before.

Advertising executive James Webb Young described this decades ago: new ideas emerge from new combinations of existing elements. That has an important implication for designers. The quality of the connections we make depends on what we expose ourselves to. Yet when we’re asked to solve a problem, one of the first things we often do is benchmark competitors. We study similar products, familiar patterns and established solutions. There is value in that.

But if we all start with the same references, ask the same questions and look in the same places, we shouldn’t be surprised when we arrive at the same answers.

I want designers to look elsewhere. If you’re working on a banking experience, perhaps the most interesting inspiration won’t come from another bank. It might come from a game, a museum, a restaurant or the way an airport manages complex journeys. The point isn’t to borrow something because it looks interesting. It’s to understand the principle behind it and ask whether it could solve a completely different problem. Sometimes the most creative contribution isn’t a new solution at all. It’s recognising that we’ve been asking the wrong question.

Pixar didn’t invent computers. It didn’t invent animation or storytelling. It connected those things and helped create a new form of filmmaking. That’s what creativity needs: curiosity, different references and the willingness to look beyond the obvious. Don’t just become better at looking for answers. Become more curious about where you look. Because if you only look where everyone else is looking, don’t be surprised when you create what everyone else is creating.

System: Seeing the whole, not just the screen

An old parable tells of three stonecutters working on the same building. A traveller asks the first what he is doing. “I’m earning a living,” he replies. The second takes pride in his workmanship: he wants to be the best stonecutter in the country. The third looks up and says, “I’m building a cathedral.” The story appears in Peter Drucker’s The Practice of Management. All three are doing essentially the same work. What changes is how much of the whole they can see.

I think about that story when I look at the work happening in a design team. Imagine a designer asked to create an icon. They explore a few directions, refine the details and deliver a beautiful icon. There is nothing wrong with that. I want designers who care about every curve, every proportion and every pixel. But I also want someone to stop and ask, “Hang on. Why do we need this icon in the first place?” Maybe it duplicates something that already exists. Maybe the problem is the way the experience has been organised. Maybe the iconography system itself needs to evolve. If all you ask is for a better icon, you may get a better icon. You may never discover that you didn’t need one.

A designer should be able to change altitude. At one level, there is the icon. Zoom out and you see the iconography system, then the design language, the product and the organisation behind it. Keep going and you find the technology, operations, policies and people that make the experience possible.

But seeing the bigger picture isn’t enough. You have to question it. “That’s how we’ve always done it” is not an explanation. Neither is “That’s what I was asked to design.” Go and meet the people whose work connects to yours. Understand what happens before someone reaches your screen and what happens after they leave it. Learn which constraints are real and which ones have simply survived because nobody thought to question them.

And that brings me back to the cathedral. I don’t want designers to stop caring about the brick. I want them to care deeply about the brick while understanding what they are building, how it all fits together and whether the wall should be there at all. The best designers can obsess over a detail without becoming trapped inside it. Lay the brick well. But know the cathedral you’re building.

Method: Developing your own recipe

Chef Massimo Bottura once said, “Recipes are not meant to be followed literally.” I like that idea because it doesn’t reject technique. Quite the opposite. Before you can improvise in a kitchen, you need to understand ingredients, proportions, temperature, timing and technique. A recipe gives you a structure for learning those things. But knowing how to follow a recipe is not the same as knowing how to cook. At some point, you need to know what to change, what to leave out and what to substitute. You need to know when to follow the recipe exactly, and when what you are trying to create requires something completely different.

I think about design methods in much the same way. Over the years, I have reviewed hundreds of portfolios, and after a while you start to notice something strange. Different designer. Different company. Different problem. Same case study. Here is the brief. Here are the personas. Here are the pain points. Here is the journey map. Then comes ideation, prioritisation, wireframes and, finally, the polished interface. There is nothing wrong with any of those tools. What bothers me is when I cannot understand why they were used.

Somewhere along the way, we started confusing knowing the design process with knowing how to design.

We taught people the Double Diamond, Design Thinking, research methods, workshops, journey maps, prioritisation frameworks and countless other tools. All of them can be incredibly useful. But they are tools. Knowing the toolkit is literacy. Method is knowing what to pick, what to leave out, in what order, and why. Not every problem deserves the same process. Sometimes you know enough to go from A to B, execute it well and ship it. Sometimes the fastest way forward is to make something, test it, learn and try again. And sometimes you genuinely don’t understand the problem yet, and weeks or months of research may be exactly what is needed. The skill is not performing a prescribed process. It’s choosing the route the problem deserves, and being able to explain why.

AI can now help us perform almost every step of that process faster. It can synthesise research, map journeys, generate concepts, prototype solutions and analyse feedback. But doing all of that faster doesn’t tell you whether you needed to do it in the first place. A beautifully generated journey map is still unnecessary if you never needed a journey map.

Method was never about producing the artefacts. It was about understanding what you need to learn next, and choosing the best way to learn it.

So I don’t want designers to become experts at following a design process. I want them to build a repertoire. Learn the methods. Understand why they exist and what each one can reveal. Use them enough to know their strengths and limitations. Then develop the confidence to combine them, shorten them, extend them, reorder them or leave them out completely. A great chef doesn’t ignore the recipe because they never learned it. They can move beyond it because they understand it deeply enough to know what can change. Learn the process. Then develop your own recipe.

Ingenuity: Finding a way when there is no obvious path

When Mathieu Kassovitz was making La Haine in 1995, he knew exactly how he wanted his film to look: black and white. There was just one problem. The television broadcasters financing it wanted colour. Without their financing, there might not be a film at all. So Kassovitz shot it in colour, but released it in cinemas in black and white. If it failed, broadcasters could still show it in colour on television. It didn’t. Kassovitz won Best Director at Cannes, and La Haine became one of the defining films of French cinema. He didn’t abandon his vision or ignore the constraint. He found a way through it. That’s ingenuity.

I sometimes tell people on my team something they don’t necessarily expect to hear from a design leader: “You need to hustle.” I remember one project that wasn’t progressing. Stakeholders weren’t responding. Approvals were taking too long. There were dependencies everywhere. None of those problems was imaginary. But explaining why something couldn’t happen had started to replace figuring out how to make it happen. Hustle doesn’t mean ignoring the rules or working longer hours. It means finding another way. If the email isn’t working, have a conversation. If someone can’t make the decision, find out who can. If you don’t have everything you need, start with what you have.

I think there is a particular kind of productive stubbornness that separates people who consistently make things happen from those who wait for the circumstances to become favourable.

Designers should be particularly good at this. We spend our careers solving problems, questioning assumptions and working through constraints. Yet sometimes we stop doing exactly that when the obstacle becomes organisational. There is a difference between recognising a dependency and becoming dependent on it. “We don’t have clarity,” I hear. “I don’t have clarity either. Our job is to create it.” Ask better questions. Bring the right people together. Make a recommendation. Put something tangible in front of people so they can react to it.

We are problem solvers. That includes solving the problems that prevent us from solving the problem.

That’s the difference between creativity, method and ingenuity. Creativity helps us imagine possibilities. Method helps us choose a route. Ingenuity is what happens when the idea meets reality and the route is blocked. Kassovitz knew what he wanted to create. His ingenuity was finding a way to make it happen without pretending the constraints didn’t exist. Don’t just tell me why it can’t be done. Help me find a way.

Business: Making design matter

“Being good in business is the most fascinating kind of art. Making money is art and working is art and good business is the best art.” Andy Warhol

Andy Warhol understood something that creatives sometimes struggle with: business and creativity are not enemies. He was one of the defining artists of the twentieth century, but he also understood business exceptionally well. He came from commercial illustration, built a studio around his practice, took commissions, published a magazine, produced films and music, and turned his own name into a brand. For Warhol, business wasn’t something happening around the art. Business was part of the art.

There is something designers can learn from that. Great design doesn’t exist in isolation. It has to survive an organisation. It has to convince people. It has to operate within constraints, create value and ultimately produce an outcome. Yet there is one sentence I hear surprisingly often from designers, particularly design leaders: “I don’t have a seat at the table.” Ah, yes. The table. Designers really love the table. Why am I not invited? Why was Design not involved? Why are they bringing us in now, when everything has already been decided? I hear it from my own team often enough that sometimes I wonder whether my job is to lead Design or manage seating arrangements.

But then we finally get into the room, and immediately position ourselves on the other side of it. We arrive carrying the flag of user-centricity. “But what about the user?” And we should. The problem begins when being the voice of the user turns into believing we are the only people in the room with a legitimate point of view. We did the research. We spoke to the users. Therefore, we are right. Suddenly the conversation becomes Design versus Business. We talk constantly about empathy. Yet sometimes our empathy stops the moment the user does.

Empathy cannot stop with the user. Understand the business with the same curiosity you use to understand the people you design for.

What is the organisation trying to achieve? How does it create value? What does this decision cost? What are the constraints? Who is accountable if it goes wrong? The person disagreeing with your beautiful idea may not hate good design. They may simply be accountable for something you haven’t taken the time to understand. That doesn’t mean surrendering the user perspective. Challenge the business. Debate it. Fight for the experience when it matters. But understand what you are challenging.

The best designers don’t choose between the user and the business. They understand both well enough to find a better answer.

And that is also my answer to the famous seat at the table. Stop waiting for someone to give it to you. Earn it. Learn the business. Read the strategy. Understand the numbers, priorities and constraints. Spend time with people outside Design. Learn their language rather than expecting everyone to learn yours. And when you present design, don’t only explain why it is better for the user. Explain why it matters. What becomes easier? What becomes cheaper? What becomes faster? What risk disappears? What value does it create? The moment you can have that conversation, you are no longer the designer asking to be included in the business conversation. You are part of it.

Which brings me back to Warhol. He didn’t become less of an artist because he understood business. His understanding of business helped his work travel further and become more consequential. The same is true for design. Mastering business doesn’t make you less of a designer. It gives your design a better chance of mattering.

What happens when the machine learns?

There is an uncomfortable question hanging over everything I have just written. What happens when AI starts developing these skills too? And perhaps more importantly, what happens when it becomes better at some of them than we are?

That question is becoming less hypothetical than it sounds. Google’s AI Co-Scientist, for example, has been designed to generate scientific hypotheses, evaluate competing explanations and make connections across large bodies of existing knowledge. In one case, it independently proposed a hypothesis that matched a mechanism researchers had spent years investigating. Creativity. Systems thinking. Method. Perhaps even something resembling instinct. I don’t know where that leads. And I wouldn’t be surprised if, in a few years, some of the things I have described throughout this article become capabilities we routinely expect from machines.

But I don’t think that makes these skills any less important for us to practise. We shouldn’t develop creativity because machines cannot be creative. We shouldn’t develop taste because machines will never learn to judge. We shouldn’t practise our craft because AI will never master it. Those are increasingly dangerous assumptions to make.

We should develop these skills because developing them develops us. Creativity makes us curious about where we look. Craft teaches us to care about what we make. Taste forces us to form a point of view. Instinct grows through experience. Systems thinking teaches us to look beyond what is immediately in front of us. Method teaches us to question the route. Ingenuity teaches us to find another one when it disappears. Business teaches us to understand the world our ideas have to survive in. These things are worth practising regardless of what a machine can eventually do.

Because perhaps the real danger isn’t that machines become more like us. It’s that, as machines become more capable, we allow ourselves to become more like machines. Waiting for instructions. Accepting the first answer. Following the process without questioning it. Producing without thinking. Outsourcing our judgement because something else can do it faster.

So use the tools. Learn them. Push them. Let them challenge you. Let them make you faster and extend what you are capable of doing. But keep training the runner underneath. Keep thinking. Keep questioning. Keep making unexpected connections. Keep developing your judgement.

Because the machine will keep getting better. You should too. Otherwise, you’re just a machine.

title: After the AI bubble: a manifesto
text:
After the AI bubble: a manifesto

Computers should be tools for the people but — hidden in a malaise of fatalism — the AI bubble has made computers tools to push people around. Soon, or in some time, this will change. We have some thoughts to share with you in the meantime.

Preamble

The purpose of computers is human freedom. — Ted Nelson
  1. We are not “anti-AI.” We are against abuse, destruction, and exploitation: of people and our environment, as well as lies and manipulation that provide cover for the above.
  2. We are unsatisfied with the confusing, inaccurate term “artificial intelligence” (AI), but grimly accept it because it is widely-used.
  3. Our demands relate primarily to economic relationships, discourse and information software; we don’t see concerns we omit — such as regarding the environment and material created by AI (“slop”) — as less important, only out of focus; if you are prepared to complete the picture, contact us.
  4. We are enthusiastic about the real potential of AI and large language models (LLMs), but think that their capabilities have been overstated.
  5. We all have a horse in this race: from alternative technologies seeking customers to alternative worldviews seeking adherents.
  6. We think that the overriding character of AI today is that of a speculative bubble: at a scale for which any possible outcome will bring significant hardship — we must avoid a disaster like that which followed similar periods, particularly the 1920s and 30s.
  7. We think we can build a future that protects individual liberty and the general welfare by — among other things — using computers more humanely.
  8. Our manifesto will be stronger with your feedback and comments: please provide them.
  9. And, if you agree, please comment to sign your name.

Argument

1. Economics: an AI bubble

We are in a bubble. Generative AI does not do the things that it’s being sold as doing, and the things it can actually do aren’t the kind of things that create business returns, automate labor, or really do much more than one extension of a cloud software platform. The money isn’t there, the users aren’t there, every company seems to lose money and some companies lose so much money that it’s impossible to tell how they’ll survive. — Ed Zitron
We have a history of net losses and may not generate sufficient revenue to achieve or sustain profitability in the future. — Anthropic (October 2026, draft S-1 filing)

The current AI bubble — perhaps best charted by Ed Zitron — is the largest in a series of tech bubbles: dot-com, crypto, with overlapping sub-bubbles like “web3” and “metaverse.” Though Open AI CEO Sam Altman has called the economic conditions around AI a bubble, many disagree, or agree that we are in a bubble but claim that this is not a problem.

Bubbles happen when excitement about a speculative investment (which can be in anything, from shares in public companies to flowers) takes on a life of its own, and investments pile in more due to momentum than the desire to build something useful.

Bubbles are neatly regressive: putting money in the pockets of those who got in early and got out early, fleecing those whose who came late to the party, with onlookers shouldering the economic fallout. Bubbles precede our most cataclysmic economic moments and the succeeding social conflicts, most obviously the roaring 20s — great depression—authoritarianism/WWII cycle.

However, many have argued that the AI bubble is a good thing, because we might get something useful out of it, such as the “dark fiber” laid down during the dot-com bubble.

There is, of course, nothing close to a guarantee that anything of the sort will happen. Datacenters, much in demand today and often cited as a useful asset that could come out of this bubble, are quite unlike fiber (which is essentially incorruptible glass buried beneath the street):

  1. Datacenters are highly specific to AI loads which may go away
  2. And wear out

Mistakes that turn out to be profitable, like dark fiber, aren’t arguments for bubbles; something either has a strong argument for it in the moment or was unjustifiable in the moment, and it paying off was merely good fortune.

Bubbles and crashes are failures of planning and capital allocation. If bubbles were actually desirable, it would be possible to find a bubble proponent who would tolerate one in an economy they control, e.g. their household or within their own company. Rather, bubbles are good only when someone else picks up the tab.

For those who think all this investment is quite sensible, i.e. that we are not in a bubble, one must ask: given that the U.S. economy would likely be in recession without AI, what are we doing this for?

Isn’t the rest of the economy — farming, transportation, healthcare, arts, etc. — the place where the actual purported benefits of AI will reach us? The gains in productivity and innovation promised by AI-proponents must be delivered to us through things. How long, therefore, should we stifle the rest of the economy while we wait to AI to pay off? And what will be left?

Bubbles hurt when they burst, but usually the sooner the burst comes the better, as bigger bubbles hurt more. Finding a way to avoid popping the bubble — such as through state intervention — stands protect those invested, while keeping the capital allocated to the wrong places.

We need to leave behind an economic regime buoyed by a series of fast-growing and capital-intensive fads, and transition to a stabler economy with broader investments and benefits.

2. Messaging: fatalism, hype, and “CEO said”

The greatest myth of technology is the myth of determinism: the belief that technology is determinate, objective, inevitable, that the nature of computers is given. […] The computer world deals with imaginary, made-up stuff that was all made up by somebody. Everything you see was designed and put there by someone. — Ted Nelson
The most important thing about a gadget isn’t what it does; it’s who it does it for and who it does it to. — Cory Doctorow

We have internalized the narrative that the way computers work is preordained, and that it is necessary that computers work the way they do currently. We can thank this narrative for the idea that AI is the next step in computing.

This puts us in a malaise of fatalism, making it easy to believe that we must accept what we are given — including LLMs and AI — or risk being left behind. We — the people — create technology and computers; we could drive it in a different direction if we wish or abolish it altogether. If people are being left behind, other people are leaving them behind, not technology.

It’s easy to see technology as something like the laws of nature — offering us gifts like solar power or antibiotics — but it also shares a great deal with fashion: a succession of trends, driven not just by utility, but significantly by imitation and novelty. Packaged technology — like computers, operating systems, applications — has much much more to do with peers and predecessors in their category and with cultural norms regarding how we work with information than it have to do with logic and physics.

Ignore — as Cory Doctrow advises in The Reverse Centaur’s Guide to Life After AI — those who say “there is no alternative” (TINA). IBM said there was no alternative to the mainframe, and DEC proved overwise with the minicomputer and later Apple with the microcomputer; Microsoft said there is no alternative to Windows and Linus Torvalds proved otherwise with Linux.

AI fatalism rides along with two other ideas:

  1. AI will save the world (e.g. cure cancer).
  2. AI will destroy the world (e.g. kill us in a “Terminator-style” scenario).

These are really two sides of the same idea: that AI will, sometime in the future, attain awe-inspiring abilities and change the fate or our species. These claims are usually broached in terms familiar to most people but without practical specifics, or are otherwise nonsensical.

This serves to distract people from real questions relevant to AI today — whether and how to implement AI, how to handle datacenters, whom to complain to that you have to talk to a machine to get customer service, how to protect your data, how to respond to slop — and have them focus instead on fantasies.

This distraction gains much ground thanks to “CEO said” journalism, first christened by Chris Kottke, wherein journals will print nonsense if a CEO said it. Journalists have a moral obligation to challenge the facts and perspectives of their subjects, and especially the executives of influential and well-capitalized companies.

We should evaluate AI and any other technology on its merits, without distraction from fatalism, hype and nonsense.

3. Humanity: pretend AI personalities

You’ll have these little “Max Headroom” characters with bow ties, who you have to talk to. […] Having to deal socially with inane objects that pretend to understand you, but don’t, is much worse than a cocktail party. It’s absolutely unnecessary; it’s a council of despair. — Ted Nelson

We anthropomorphize everything, and technology companies are quick to encourage this: from the original Macintosh’s jaunty mouth, to Microsoft’s Clippy.

Large language models are so good at talking that many truly believe them to be conscious or to have personalities. LLMs have neither personhood nor personality: monitoring them to use and respond to first person pronouns is deceptive — more so, say, than Clippy because LLMs are so good at talking.

Names and personal pronouns are for intelligent beings with personalities: having people use them for LLMs puts the user in a posture of equality with the machine, which, given the growing power-imbalance between the supercorporations fielding LLMs and people, puts the machine above the human in the power relationship.

Conversely, we and our corporations and governments find it just as easy to dehumanize people: sometimes through lurid oppression, sometimes merely through bureaucratic drudgery. It is not fair to expect someone hanging onto their dignity by a thread to talk to a machine as though it has a personality (more so to require them to do) in order to proceed with whatever work, government or customer service task is required of them.

The prospectus of the LLM includes a promise to help users manage information: particularly to find the information they need, or to contextualize their work. Such solutions, however, rarely actually organize the underlying information.

While people are making some progress, such as with graph databases and markdown files, AI’s insights are typically not stored (nor is the underlying information modified) as durable links/folders/database rows, to shape information for a future date or for other people. While AI can work between silos (e.g. large information repositories like Drive and SharePoint) it creates no workable, standalone connections between them.

LLMs promote personality at the expense of durability and interoperability. AI gives users the impression that something conscious is helping them to get organized, while their (and our society’s) information’s chaos deepens.

Machines are tools: they should respond predictably to unambiguous inputs. Putting a human persona on a machine does nothing but diminish the real human.

4. Information: siren servers and the new enclosure

An economy where advertisers thrive while journalists and artists struggle, reflects the values of a society more interested in deception and manipulation than in truth and beauty .— Jaron Lanier

In Who Owns the Future?, philosopher Jaron Lanier laid out his theory of the “siren server” — that modern companies have developed a new business model, which generates a competitive advantage by having more data and thus greater insights to leverage.

This is a new form of competitiveness: it is not the same advantage that was afforded, say, to IBM by its huge network of relationships, partnerships and salespeople; or its ability to spend colossal sums on research and development.

Siren servers do not compete by innovating (at least not when they’re mature) — they compete by being big. As a result, siren servers are incentivized to get as big as possible, as quickly as possible, leading to business practices directly misaligned with user needs:

  1. Free/artificially low pricing to enroll users, who are then monetized by degrading the performance of the service and/or by new fees. (Don’t confuse this tactic for the “free trial” approach; the siren server fees are a surprise.)
  2. Barriers to leaving, such as incompatibility (e.g. enterprise information management solutions that cannot talk to each other).
  3. Invasive advertising.

Some siren server systems felt like progress at the time, but with any kind of hindsight, this is not progress. As Doctrow outlines in Enshittification, would anyone claim, for instance, that:

  1. Today’s large, closed social networks would be worse if they allowed some measure of interoperability, e.g. that one could message one’s friends there without an account (as one can with email)?
  2. People like to be followed around by advertisers?
  3. People feel good about or don’t have a bad taste in their mouth from having rushed onto free/cheap platforms in the 2010s, to find those platforms turned into cattle-pens?

It’s arguable that modern LLM companies represent the perfection of the siren server model. They aggregate incomprehensible volumes of data, in order to deliver an informational advantage to their users.

As Lanier has also observed, this results in a peculiar and new type of economic displacement: of workers (e.g. translators, writers, designers, etc.) by tools that simulate them.

Lanier points to the example of translators, who have been obviated significantly by translation AIs that used their translations as raw material. The fact of simulation is critical: AI doesn’t displace people with a new tool — unlike and regardless of the moral nature, say, of replacing horses with cars or canals with trains — today, thousands of people have been and will be displaced by simulations based on their work.

Currently, no legal protections exist, as Doctrow explains in Reverse Centaur. There is much discussion of copyright, but this relates primarily to AI firms’ illegal use of copyright material, i.e. downloading without paying for it. We face a new question: how should we treat the aggregation of people’s material to form systems which then put the same people out of the job?

Throughout human history, we have created new rights to respond to new situations: working time, copyright, patents, zoning, etc. Copyright, for instance, became relevant after the printing press made reproducing texts inexpensive. In some cases, like working hours, many unions and managers have come to acceptable settlements. (Though there is still much to discuss.)

In other cases, such changes gave way to colossal and irrevocable wealth transfers. Perhaps the most relevant example was the enclosures in Britain. For centuries, poor farmers had the right to graze cattle on the commons — land then considered inferior for farming but still useful for the people to support themselves.

As agricultural technology improved, this land became profitable and, over several centuries, landowners enclosed the commons and denied commoners the right to graze. There are still commoners and there is still common land, but this displacement was large enough to cause the exodus from the countryside to the cities which peopled the industrial revolution.

Large organizations are launching an enclosure today: they are aggregating information we thought had no value, and giving it a value. We think that we should form a new settlement (for instance Lanier’s “data as labor”) which provides both for the right of individuals and groups to scrape and study information (including “training” AI) and for the people to make something of their newly valuable data.

Beyond this, we need to wake up to the fact that anything we create can potentially be used as “training data” and therefore must never again simply create (and share) something without first asking who will use it, whether we approve of that usage, and whether therefore it requires protection.

5. AI by force, and as force

An interface is humane if it is responsive to human needs and considerate of human frailties. — Jef Raskin

All tech companies are fond of making us aware of their new features. Companies are fond also of pushing unwanted new features, such as by taking up screen space previously available for other uses, or making a feature that previously stood alone accessible only via a new one. This has reached its zenith with AI.

Appealing to the idea that software should help the user, and should act as a tool, software should not interfere, block, or interpose itself between the user and their work. (This is distinct from “doing precisely what they want, immediately” because software is duty-bound to protect a user from accidentally deleting their writing, for instance.)

Software companies can make people aware of new AI (and other) features without violating the contract set out above. Meanwhile, users should have access to simple, conventional data access features: such as searching, filtering, results lists and tables when companies can make (and have previously made) them available.

Bosses also frequently insist that employees use AI, and some job applications make AI-use a criteria (rarely for the application itself, ironically). Given the harm and uncertainty wrought by AI, bosses should afford conscientious objectors respect and possibly rights, as we do for people with their views on war, social relationships, the environment, etc.

Meanwhile — as part of a broader trend to deny users access to effective customer service (hiding phone numbers/contact information, customer help labyrinths) — companies are now making customer service available only through AI, and are scaling down their human teams. Companies have every right to deploy tools to help (some people prefer AI customer support) but not to remove avenues of communication and accountability, especially in situations where only humans can provide meaningful help.

Software should help its users, companies should help their customers and respect their employees — let us not let AI confuse straightforward questions.

Demands

Therefore, we demand an end to:

  1. The AI bubble.
  2. Fatalism, hype, and to “CEO said” journalism.
  3. Pretend software personalities, possessed by AI or otherwise.
  4. Siren servers — companies that compete only through size and data aggregation.
  5. Companies forcing AI on users, to bosses forcing AI on employees, and of AI as a barrier between people and organizations.

And, in their place, we demand:

  1. Sustainable, broad-based economic growth with broad benefits.
  2. Sound, grounded, factual discourse on AI.
  3. The choice to use conventional information retrieval interfaces.
  4. A new settlement to remunerate people for the use of their newly valuable data.
  5. The right to object to AI and to be afforded reasonable protections for doing so.

Coda: why are we here?

Untold reams of paper, not to mention U.S. Federal money, has gone to waste on the tall tales of artificial intelligence. […] People want control over their computers and their lives. So far, even the supposedly-controllable software is uncontrollable; would you trust today’s developers to create things you can understand even less? — Ted Nelson

Estimates vary, but it’s likely that knowledge workers spend around 20% of every workday just looking for information. Generally, computer users complain that:

  1. They cannot find the information they need on their computer or in the cloud.
  2. Projects get out of hand and become unmanageable, and are often abandoned.
  3. Their work, especially in collaboration with others, is hampered by the fact that different file types and information systems don’t work together.
  4. Generally, their ideas aren’t shaped like documents and spreadsheets.

How did we get here? Ted Nelson theorizes that “it all went wrong at Xerox PARC.” PARC: where in the public imagination the ideas behind modern computing like windows, the mouse pointer, text editing, etc. were developed.

At PARC, the computer — a machine capable of creating and associating information in any way — became a machine instead for undertaking minor secretarial tasks like creating and filing paper documents, rather than building ideas. People feel like they need AI because today’s software isn’t up to the task of expressing, organizing and connecting our ideas.

Users are looking for better tools to help them get organized because our information systems destroy information; companies hold out AI as the solution, when in fact it is part of the same mistake, and will make users’ problems much much worse.

Rather, we need a new approach, that:

  1. Lets users own and control their data.
  2. Puts up no barriers between information systems (folders on your drive versus database), datatypes (e.g. document versus email) and repositories (SharePoint versus Drive).
  3. Allows users to create a growing, adapting web of durable, shareable relationships between their ideas.

After the AI bubble bursts — or otherwise when we can look at computers with clarity — let us devote the energy and creativity we need to build software subtle enough to conform to the shape of human thought.

After the AI bubble: a manifesto was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Berrypicking still beats the single answer for search, even in the world of AI
text:
Berrypicking still beats the single answer for search, even in the world of AI

In 1989 Marcia Bates showed that people search by gathering, shifting, and revising as they go. Her ideas explain what AI still misses and what is still relevant from research done 47 years ago.

Much of what product teams are learning about artificial intelligence search, an information scientist wrote down before the web existed. Marcia J. Bates spent her career at UCLA studying how people search and her 1989 paper, The Design of Browsing and Berrypicking Techniques for the Online Search Interface, argued that real searches wander, change shape, and collect value in pieces.

She aimed it at library databases that assumed one query and one best result; AI turns this on its head.

The chat box makes the same assumption, only faster.

Bates is still relevant in the age of artificial intelligence, arguably more than ever. Large language models changed what a system can answer but they didn’t change how a person goes about asking, which still means starting vague, learning while reading, and changing direction midway.

I had the pleasure of meeting her at the IA Summit in Chicago in 2018 — she most politely asked if we could have lunch and I brought a few others. It became a great conversation where I still learned concepts that I apply today, and they are incredibility relevant to what we’re doing with AI back when my company was only applying machine learning.

I’ve used her concepts to frame search and artificial intelligence summarization in legal tech software. Anyone designing search or summarization should be thanking her.

Five of her ideas hold up, each tied to a decision you’re making now.

Support Evolving Searches

Bates built the berrypicking paper as an attack on the classic retrieval model, which treats a search as one query matched once against a database to produce one best set of results.

Her objection fit in one line: “typical search queries are not static, but rather evolve.”

People begin with one reference or a narrow slice of a bigger topic, read what comes back, and let each find reshape the question.

She named the bit-at-a-time collecting after picking huckleberries scattered through a forest. Marti Hearst later made the model a standard reference for interface designers in Models of the Information Seeking Process.

The need itself shifts as the person learns, and that separates berrypicking from search methods that look similar from the outside:

  • Known-item lookup. You know what you want, such as a fact or a file, and one query finds it or doesn’t. You can accomplish this usually in a single term.
  • Iterative refinement. You rephrase to hit a fixed target, the job Gerard Salton’s relevance feedback automated. The words change, but the need doesn’t.
  • Browsing. You glimpse, sample, and pick within one place. Bates treated it as one move inside a larger search, not the same thing.
  • Berrypicking. The need evolves, and the answer arrives in pieces from many sources rather than as one final set.

That last difference is why a successful search is so hard to define:

  • The classic model let researchers score one result set for precision and recall.
  • A berrypicking search has no single set to score, and Bates called knowing when to stop one of the fundamental problems of search strategy.
  • A thumbs-up on one chat answer measures the last berry, not the picking.

Sometimes what matters most is what isn’t found.

An empty patch tells a berrypicker something, whether it’s no earlier case on point, no conflicting clause in a contract, or no research on a question. A system that always produces a confident answer hides that signal, because it never lets the absence show.

The chat window rewards the user who already knows exactly what they want, which is the user who needs the least help.

Language models repeat the classic assumption.

In LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation, a 2025 study of more than 200,000 simulated conversations, every top model tested did worse when a task arrived in pieces, with an average drop of 39 percent across six tasks. The models guessed early and didn’t recover.

The design job is to support the person whose question is still forming. Show what has shifted since the first prompt, and let people revise early assumptions without starting over.

Bates even sketched the tooling in 1989: a temporary store where searchers could flag findings as they went.

Expose Search Tactics

A decade earlier, Bates published Information Search Tactics, which won her field’s best paper award the following year. A tactic, in her definition, is a move made to further a search.

She named 29 of them in four groups, including these:

  • Check. Compare the current search against the original request.
  • Pinpoint. Narrow to the most precise terms.
  • Parallel. Broaden with synonyms and related terms.
  • Trace. Mine what you’ve already found for new terms.
  • Record. Track the trails you followed and the ones you meant to revisit.

Her premise was that naming a tactic makes it easier to reach for. Reference librarians used many of these moves without names, which left beginners no easy way to learn them.

The web repeated the problem.

People had to learn to search like Google, stripping questions down to two or three keywords and adding quotes or a minus sign when results went wrong. They’re doing the same with chat now, working out by trial and error which phrasings get a useful answer.

A blank prompt box ships with none of them, so people improvise.

Nielsen Norman Group documented one improvisation in Accordion Editing and Apple Picking: Early Generative-AI User Behaviors.

Users copied part of an earlier response into a new prompt by hand, because the interface gave them no other way to point at it. It’s berrypicking with copy and paste as the only tool.

That’s a search behavior, because chat and search are closer than they look. In both, a person puts a need into words, the system matches it against stored information, and the person judges what comes back and tries again.

Retrieval-augmented assistants run a search behind the scenes and summarize the results, so the biggest difference is the shape of the reply: a list of links in one, a paragraph in the other.

Everything Bates learned about searching also applies to chatting in spades.

Missing controls matter most for experts, who read a bad result set as a clue rather than a verdict. They tighten, exclude, widen, and re-sort in small passes until the set matches what they meant, and they decide when it’s done. In Investigating the Querying and Browsing Behavior of Advanced Search Engine Users, Ryen White and Dan Morris found marked differences between people who used query operators and those who didn’t, in how they queried, clicked, browsed, and fared.

Faceted search is the interface version of those moves.

In a study reported in Hearst’s chapter Integrating Navigation with Search, 91 percent of 32 art history students preferred a faceted image interface to a plain one, even though it was slower.

A chat reply hides exactly those facets and filters, when most of Bates’s 29 tactics could become buttons nobody has to phrase.

Choose the Automation Level

In 1990, Bates asked the question every agent team is now answering under deadline: Where Should the Person Stop and the Information Search Interface Start? Her answer was a scale.

  • At level 0 the system offers no help.
  • Level 1 explains possible moves
  • Level 2 carries them out on command
  • Level 3 watches the search and suggests next steps
  • Level 4 runs the whole search, either explaining its choices or just returning results.

In product terms, the levels are easy to spot:

  • Level 1 is a help panel that lists search operators
  • Level 2 is a filter that runs when you click it
  • Level 3 is a “did you mean” correction or a suggested follow-up question.
  • Level 4 is the research agent that disappears for several minutes and comes back with a finished report.

She argued that research had fixated on level 4, while many searchers wanted the speed of automation and control of strategy. Jakob Nielsen called generative tools AI: First New UI Paradigm in 60 Years in 2023, describing a reversal of the locus of control in which users state the outcome and the computer picks the method.

Bates had mapped that reversal decades earlier, and put most of the useful ground short of the far edge.

Most AI products jump straight to level 4 and call the result an agent. That’s not right.

Skipping the middle skips the levels where trust gets built. People defer to the machine even when it’s wrong, which I document in the Automation Bias entry on UX Guidelines, a reference site I maintain. Pick the level per task, and let people move the dial.

Fix the Content Layers

Her 2002 paper The Cascade of Interactions in the Digital Library Interface lists the layers under any search experience: infrastructure, content, metadata, indexing, and the search engine, with the interface and the person at the top.

Decisions at each layer ripple upward, and good interface design can’t rescue weak choices further down.

Swap “digital library” for “retrieval-augmented assistant” and little changes. Above the model is the chat window your team keeps polishing. Below it are document stores, chunking rules, and permissions someone set up years ago for another purpose. Good metadata is what sets context for the model, telling it what a document is, who it applies to, and whether it’s still current. The demo runs on 20 clean documents, and production meets a decade of duplicate policies and unlabeled drafts.

A semantic layer goes a step further.

It defines what terms mean and how they relate, so “customer,” “client,” and “account holder” resolve to the same thing, and the model works from shared definitions instead of guessing.

Bates proposed something close to this in 1986: a cluster thesaurus that gathered every variant of a concept under one entry, so a search on any term could reach them all.

A fluent answer built on a bad index is still a bad answer.

Gartner predicted in Lack of AI-Ready Data Puts AI Projects at Risk, a February 2025 release, that through 2026 organizations will abandon 60 percent of artificial intelligence projects that lack ready data. That’s a forecast, but the same release reported that 63 percent of organizations lacked the right data practices or weren’t sure they had them.

This is the uncomfortable part for designers. The quality of a search result, or of a generative answer, is the user experience, and no polish around it makes up for a weak one.

Your influence has to reach down the cascade into labeling and indexing, and Bates argued the specialists for every layer had to design together.

Design for Browsing

Bates returned to browsing in 2007 with What Is Browsing — Really? A Model Drawing From Behavioural Science Research. Browsing, she argued, is a series of glimpses: you take in a field of view, select something, examine it, then keep it or drop it, and repeat.

She traced it to the exploratory behavior animals use to find food and shelter, which is why nobody needs to be taught how.

Similarly, I’ve been through 65 airports, partly to see how cities tell people where things are. The good terminals let you take in the whole hall at once, spot the sign you need, and change course without asking anyone. That’s the opposite of waiting at the information desk for one answer.

Generative search is quietly moving people toward the desk.

Pew Research Center tracked the browsing of 900 U.S. adults in March 2025 and reported that Google Users Are Less Likely to Click on Links When an AI Summary Appears in the Results. Visits with a summary led to a result click 8 percent of the time, against 15 percent without one, and sessions ended outright on 26 percent of summary pages versus 16 percent elsewhere.

Some of that is the summary doing its job. Some is a person who never glimpsed the source they didn’t know to ask for. So keep the scene around the answer, with neighboring sources and related threads, so the glimpse still has somewhere to land.

Conclusion

None of these ideas came from studying artificial intelligence. They came from watching people in libraries, card catalogs, and early online databases, and that’s exactly why they hold.

The technology between a person and the information keeps changing. The person mostly doesn’t.

Read together, Bates’s five ideas make one argument. Search is something people do over time, using moves they choose, at a level of control they want, on top of layers they never see. Their eyes do more of the work than any query. Every piece of that is a design decision, and most current products make it by default.

She also left what I’d call the berrypicking test for any assistant on your roadmap. Does it expect the question to change, or punish the change? Does it name the moves, or make people invent them? Can the person choose how much the system decides, and does anyone own the content underneath? Is there still room to look around?

The single answer is impressive. It’s also the classic model she spent decades arguing against, with better grammar. The teams that do best with this generation of tools will design for the berrypicker, the searcher whose question hasn’t settled yet.

Action Items

  • Show question history. Keep a visible summary of what the person has asked so far, and let them edit an earlier question without starting a new chat.
  • Add refine controls. Put buttons for narrowing, excluding, broadening, and checking against the original request next to every answer, so nobody has to phrase those moves as a prompt.
  • Set automation per task. Decide which tasks the system only suggests on and which it can run by itself, and give people a setting to change that.
  • Fix metadata first. Tag documents with type, owner, date, and status, define shared terms in a semantic layer, and show the sources behind every answer, including when nothing relevant was found.

Resources

  • Information and the Information Professions, Selected Works of Marcia J. Bates, volume I (Ketchikan Press, 2016). Her essays on what information is, including “Fundamental Forms of Information” and “The Invisible Substrate of Information Science.”
  • Information Searching Theory and Practice, Selected Works, volume II (Ketchikan Press, 2016). Collects “Information Search Tactics” and “What Is Browsing — Really?” along with her work on search techniques.
  • Information Users and Information System Design, Selected Works, volume III (Ketchikan Press, 2016). Includes the berrypicking paper and her 1990 paper on how much a search system should do for the person.
  • Understanding Information Retrieval Systems: Management, Types, and Standards (Auerbach Publications, 2012). A reference volume she edited on how retrieval systems are managed, the main types, and the standards behind them.
  • Marcia J. Bates Home Page. Her UCLA page, with free copies of many of the papers cited in this piece.

title: Native is a floor, not a ceiling
text:
Native is a floor, not a ceiling

With AI, a polished look costs nothing. Native brings what can’t be drawn, and it moves with the system, one step ahead of what imitates it.

An AI assistant helped me write this. The ideas, the experience and the final edit are mine.

In June 2025, Apple introduced Liquid Glass, the new material of iOS 26. In its WWDC session on UIKit, the company put it plainly: “Your apps get this new appearance as soon as you recompile with the new SDK.” Bars, sheets, popovers and controls: most of what comes from the system frameworks changed at once, without a designer touching it.

Apps that drew their own controls got nothing. The next day, the Flutter team replied on GitHub that it was not developing Apple’s new design in its Cupertino library, the one that imitates iOS, for now. Its documentation presents drawing your own controls as a benefit: a Flutter app “looks and feels the same on all versions of the OS, even if the OS changed the implementations of its controls.” When iOS 26 shipped on September 15, 2025, that promise of stability had turned into a visible lag. The team has since moved its libraries out of the core framework to move faster, and says work is underway on Liquid Glass, but as of November 5, 2026, the issue is still open.

I worked with that choice for a long time, for the same reasons. Drawing your own controls means owning your rendering, on every version of the system. The price is that lag at every change. As long as a polished look took work, the price was worth paying: that work is what set an app apart.

AI changes the math. A polished look now takes one prompt, and generated interfaces converge in visual appearance and layout. I wrote elsewhere about why everything ends up looking alike, what people call slop; there I called apparent quality the floor, and AI now hands it to everyone. Native is a floor of another kind, the one an image doesn’t give you. Native components don’t make an app beautiful. They keep it from looking fake, and they move with the system.

AI draws the picture of native

Since October, I have been asking several AI models to design app screens, for a study I will publish soon. They imitate the system, under certain conditions, and only what can be seen.

The first condition is naming the device. Ask for a mobile app without saying which, and you get a generic screen that doesn’t really follow either iPhone or Android. Write “iPhone”, and the switches do have the shape of iOS switches. Add the instruction to follow the platform’s current conventions, and they fix a few more things that have a name: the green of the switches, the back chevron. But a year after iOS 26 shipped, the iOS they draw is still mostly the old one. The floating tab bar and the sheets detached from the edges, the iOS 26 design, only show up with that instruction, and rarely.

My explanation: an AI learns from what already exists, and the old iOS had years to fill the web. The system, meanwhile, moves every year, a little and sometimes a lot. On iOS, a native app follows by recompiling; an imitation stays stuck on the day it was copied. It’s the counterfeit copying last year’s collection, when the fashion house has already moved on to the next one.

A study published this spring points the same way. Researchers had three AI design tools generate 138 mobile screens, without mentioning iOS or Android. The models have learned “the visual syntax of contemporary mobile interfaces”, they write: navigation conventions are almost always there. But that success, in their words, “appears to be pattern-driven rather than principle-driven”, and they report a significant gap between visual and functional usability: help, error prevention and error recovery are often missing.

What the image doesn’t show

Imitating is already a lot. But the floor is mostly behavior. The back gesture that works everywhere. The share sheet everyone recognizes. The confirmation that, on iOS 26, grows out of the button that opened it. The sheet that rises from the bottom and that you dismiss with a swipe. A screenshot shows, at best, the picture of it.

Apple says it in the branding page of its guidelines: when you use components people already know, the experience feels “immediately reliable and familiar”. A familiar control does what you expect it to.

In 1998, with desktop software, John Satzinger and Lorne Olfman showed that commands that change from one application to the next make users take more actions, while a different visual appearance tends to make them more accurate. What matters is that the way you act stays the same.

It’s like the grammar of a language: everyone shares the same one, and nobody calls it slop. Slop is the stock phrase you’ve read a hundred times.

UIKit controls also come with built-in accessibility, and system components with text that scales to the size the user picked and a layout that flips for Arabic or Hebrew. On Android, the Compose documentation says that “most accessibility support is provided with little or no additional work” by its components, Material included. A control redrawn by hand has to rebuild all of that, and nothing guarantees it will: Kate Owens, at Deque, describes a custom slider that VoiceOver “skipped over entirely and never focused”.

Louie Mantia, a former Apple icon designer and a sharp critic of Liquid Glass, put it this way in 2025, about icons: “Everyone can look decent without actually being decent.” A generated mockup can draw an alert that looks like the iOS one without saying that the iOS one should be used. Rebuilt by hand, however faithfully, it only gives the app the picture of the floor.

The more apps get built from generated mockups, the more of them will look native without being native. That’s why, in my view, native matters more today than it did yesterday. The risk lies in the copied mockup: when an AI writes the code of a native project, it can call the real components. It can also produce native slop: the real components, all left at their defaults, and nothing of the brand around them. It works and it follows the system, but it looks like every other app.

On iPhone, the difference shows

You might think users see none of this. The only controlled experiment I found that pits a native app against its cross-platform version says they do see a difference, on iPhone, as soon as they can compare.

In 2014, Esteban Angulo and Xavier Ferré had thirty-seven people test two versions of the same app, fourteen of them on iPhone. One was native, the other built with Titanium, a cross-platform tool. Asked which version best matched their idea of an app for their phone, iPhone users picked the native one 86% to 7%. On Android, the gap was much smaller: 52% to 39%.

On iPhone, the seven people who had tried the cross-platform version first found it typical of iOS; among the seven who tried it after the native one, only four did. The gap mostly shows by comparison. But the cross-platform version also displayed native components, and a different team had designed it: the study can’t tell what made the difference. Nor does it say what it’s worth in ratings or sales, and a study of nearly 12,000 Android apps concludes that native and hybrid apps (web apps in a native shell) do equally well in ratings.

The ceiling is elsewhere

Native fixes the fake, not the alike. Standing out from other apps is still the brand’s job, and the floor doesn’t prevent it. In 2019, on UX Collective, Reza Bigdeli, an Android developer, answered designers who find standard components “cheap”. His advice: follow the platform’s guidelines, and keep creativity for the web. I follow him on the floor; for the rest, an app can have a strong identity without leaving its platform’s conventions.

Apple itself doesn’t reward a single style. In 2023, its Design Awards honored Flighty and Duolingo the same year. Flighty won in the Interaction category, which rewards interfaces “perfectly tailored to their platform”. Its founder, Ryan Jones, wanted the app to work so well that it would feel “almost boringly obvious”. Duolingo, on the other hand, is a highly stylized interface, which Apple still praises for its “best-in-class design” and “easy-to-follow UI”.

For Apple, “even a highly stylized interface can be approachable if it maintains familiar behaviors and patterns.” A WWDC26 session describes an app in two layers: bars and controls rely on what people already know, the content carries the brand, and the whole rests on a “baseline of platform familiarity”. That boundary is what a generated mockup doesn’t show.

Where to spend the effort

What comes from the system: navigation, back, sharing, confirmations, sheets, controls, text size. You don’t redraw them by default: Apple advises keeping custom work for the places where it has the “biggest impact”, and warns that a utility control remade by hand can make an app look less native, or even dated. Specify them by name, so nobody rebuilds them as a picture.

What comes from the brand: the content, the typography of headings (which should also follow the size the user picked), illustration, the tone of the copy, the moments where the app surprises. That’s where the identity budget gets spent. Apple even warns against too much brand: a brand color used everywhere dilutes its impact.

When the mockup comes from an AI, name the device and its current conventions in the prompt, then review that split first. Anything that looks like a system control should at least behave like one, and the safest bet is that it is one. The rest can be as free as you like: that’s where an app stops looking like the others.

Cover image: Apple’s design kits for iOS 27, the system components every app gets. Image: Apple Developer.

Mathieu Poli is Head of Frontend Engineering at GoodBarber and writes about frontend engineering, product design and AI.
